overview: This card covers atlas id oman, an approximate 1530-1914 sequence of eleven display intervals. It is not a single unchanging state: the range crosses Portuguese-held Muscat, the Ya‘ruba imamate, Al Bu Said rule, an overseas empire and a diminished coastal sultanate. The identical 1530-1715 polygon excludes every tested Omani city, including Muscat and Nizwa. From 1783 to 1914 the shapes include only Nizwa and Duqm among the tested domestic sites; they still omit Muscat, Sohar, Sur, Salalah, Mirbat, Khasab and Buraimi. No oman shape includes tested Hormuz, Gwadar, Zanzibar, Mombasa, Lamu, Pemba or Kilwa. The later oman-1945 modern geometry finally includes most tested core cities. These are poor locators, not control maps. The 1530 start is not a founding date, and 1914 is not dissolution. Separate muscat-and-oman (1938-1945) and oman-1945 (1945-open) records leave an atlas gap from 1914 to 1938.

periods.title: Portuguese-held ports and divided inland powers
periods.summary: The atlas begins during a fragmented era: Portugal controlled Muscat while Omani communities and rulers retained varied authority beyond its forts.

periods.title: Ya‘ruba unification and the struggle for Muscat
periods.summary: Nasir bin Murshid became the first Ya‘ruba imam in 1624; Sultan bin Saif’s forces ended Portuguese rule in Muscat in 1650.

periods.title: Maritime expansion, succession war and Persian invasion
periods.summary: Ya‘ruba naval power reached East Africa, but a disputed succession fractured Oman and Persian forces occupied key places before their expulsion.

periods.title: Ahmad bin Said and early Al Bu Said rule
periods.summary: Ahmad bin Said defeated Persian forces, was elected imam and founded the ruling house conventionally dated from 1744.

periods.title: Treaties and a transoceanic sultanate
periods.summary: British and United States treaties accompanied Said bin Sultan’s Indian Ocean state, whose court and economy became deeply tied to Zanzibar.

periods.title: Succession crisis and separation from Zanzibar
periods.summary: After Said bin Sultan died, rival heirs ruled Muscat and Zanzibar; Lord Canning’s 1861 award made the inheritances separate.

periods.title: Reduced sultanate and tightening British influence
periods.summary: Muscat remained formally independent but lost Zanzibar’s wealth, relied increasingly on Britain and accepted restrictive agreements, including the 1891 territorial pledge.

periods.title: Interior imamate uprising at the atlas endpoint
periods.summary: Salim bin Rashid al-Kharusi led an Ibadi imamate uprising in 1913; British Indian forces helped defend the coastal sultanate.

sections.title: One map label, several very different political orders

items.text: The atlas opens in 1530, but “Oman” was not founded that year. Portuguese forces had appeared at Muscat in 1507 and later held fortified coastal positions, while inland towns, tribal coalitions and imams followed their own politics. A 1915 British compilation is useful for the sequence, yet its categories and spellings come from an imperial archive. The safest reading is a region with overlapping power, not a neat national polygon waiting to become modern Oman.

In 1624 Nasir bin Murshid was elected the first Ya‘ruba imam. He fought to unite rival communities and weaken Portuguese positions; his successor Sultan bin Saif captured Muscat in 1650. The achievement was political and military, not a magic moment when every corner of today’s Oman instantly obeyed one administration. It also explains a major atlas failure: the 1650 shape does not even contain the tested point for Muscat.

Victory at Muscat helped Ya‘ruba rulers build naval power toward East Africa. A disputed succession fed factional war, and Persian expeditions occupied parts of Oman in 1737-1744. Ahmad bin Said, governor of Sohar, emerged from the crisis, drove out Persian forces and was elected imam, beginning the Al Bu Said era.

Al Bu Said rule changed titles and centres without erasing the older imamate ideal. Muscat grew as the dynastic and commercial capital, while claims to elected Ibadi leadership remained powerful in the interior. A treaty with Britain in 1798 and another with the United States in 1833 expanded diplomacy and commerce. Those connections brought opportunity, but they also gave foreign powers more tools to shape Omani finance and politics.

sections.title: Indian Ocean power, cultural exchange and coerced labour

items.text: Said bin Sultan’s realm connected Muscat, ports on the Iranian and Makran coasts and a growing East African domain. Around 1840 he made Zanzibar his main court; the Omani National Museum calls this a capital transfer. Ships, sailors and merchants moved dates, fish, grain, ivory, cloves, timber and manufactured goods around the ocean. Authority was uneven and depended on ports, local partners and maritime routes, so “empire” never meant one uniform administration painted solidly across every coast.

Stone Town was not simply “Oman overseas.” UNESCO describes a Swahili trading city whose coral-rag houses, narrow streets, courtyards and carved doors blended African, Arab, Indian and European practices. Omani dynastic rule and foreign merchants reshaped it, but Swahili residents and builders were agents in its history. Its surviving architecture records exchange, inequality and local creativity; it should not be credited to a single sultan or treated as a copy of Muscat.

The empire’s prosperity carried a brutal cost. The Zanzibar nomination dossier says that by the mid-nineteenth century more than 20,000 enslaved people were being imported, with about half absorbed by island clove plantations and many others re-exported. Omani Arab owners were prominent, though not the only slaveholders. People seized from African communities produced wealth under coercion; describing cloves and ivory as ordinary “trade goods” without them would hide the human machinery of the economy.

An 1845 agreement, effective in 1847, promised to stop slave exports from the sultan’s African dominions and imports into his Asian possessions, and let British ships seize some offending vessels. Yet it explicitly excepted transport within a broad East African zone including Zanzibar, Pemba and Mafia. This was a restriction, not emancipation: it neither freed people already enslaved nor immediately ended plantation labour or trafficking. The treaty itself shows why a proclamation date must not be mistaken for lived freedom.

Said bin Sultan died in 1856, and his sons Thuwaini and Majid held Muscat and Zanzibar respectively. Lord Canning’s 1861 British arbitration declared the two inheritances distinct and required Zanzibar to pay Muscat an annual subsidy. That settlement ended the united dynastic realm; it did not end Omani families, language, religious networks or memories in East Africa. Later Zanzibar history, including the final closure of its slave market, belongs to Zanzibar’s separate political record.

After separation, the sultans of Muscat were officially independent yet increasingly depended on British money and force. In 1891 the sultan pledged not to cede, sell, mortgage or otherwise place territory under another power except Britain. Britain later supported coastal rulers against interior opponents. “Independent” and “under strong imperial influence” can both be true; calling Oman either a simple British colony or completely unconstrained misses the documented relationship.

sections.title: Forts, government, learning and water engineering

items.text: Jabreen, built in 1675 for Imam Bil‘arab bin Sultan, was more than a battle box. Its plan joined residence, government and learning: meeting rooms, a courtroom, living quarters, kitchen, date stores, guardrooms and spaces associated with administrative and religious study. It also had prisons and nasty defensive openings for pouring boiling oil or date molasses. Kid verdict: a castle where homework, court cases, dinner and extremely sticky defence could happen under one roof.

Bahla Fort is a useful warning against giving every old building to the period on this card. UNESCO dates the oasis’s great Banu Nebhan phase to the twelfth through fifteenth centuries, before the atlas’s 1530 start. Later rulers repaired and occupied parts of the complex, but the mud-brick fort, family compounds, market, mosques, sablas, bath houses and falaj form a layered settlement. It is heritage located in Oman, not a construction project of the modern sultanate or one dynasty.

Aflaj made permanent settlement possible in dry country by carrying groundwater or spring water downhill through surface and underground channels. Communities divided flow in timed shares, sometimes read against a sundial, and maintained the system together. Water supported date palms, other crops and domestic use; access was therefore economic and political power. UNESCO’s roughly 3,000 functioning systems demonstrate endurance, but its ancient origin evidence does not mean every channel visible today was dug in 500 CE, or by the rulers on this card.

A heritage description of Fiqain Fort records a seven-metre well connected through the floors and a washing or bathing basin on each level. That is clever vertical water access inside a fortified elite building, not evidence of taps in every village house. The source does not identify a universal household toilet system. When evidence is thin, the honest answer is “we do not know one standard”, much better than installing imaginary palace plumbing with a historian’s wrench.

sections.title: Homes, harvests, markets and school days

items.text: At Harat al-Sulaif, founded in the Ya‘ruba era, people shifted residence with the agricultural calendar: during the date harvest many lived among the palm gardens, returning to the fortified settlement afterward. Houses were often two-storey mud-brick buildings with courtyards and decorated rooms. The market had livestock auctions, vegetable sellers, tailors, blacksmiths and weapon makers. This is one documented community, not a template for coastal sailors, Dhofari pastoralists, enslaved workers or every Omani family.

Homes could double as family archives. At the eighteenth-century al-Bait al-‘Aod, generations wrote births, deaths and other important events upstairs; its windows and doors came from India. In Musandam, one-room lock houses stored food and water in jars too large to fit through the finished doorway, so the jars went in during construction. These museum examples show family memory, seasonal movement and ocean trade in wood and craft, plus the ancient truth that storage planning matters before you build the door.

From the seventeenth through nineteenth centuries, many children’s first formal lessons took place in kuttab, where Qur’an recitation anchored elementary learning. Students who completed that stage could join mosque circles in centres such as Nizwa, Rustaq, Bahla, al-Mudhaibi and al-Hamra for religious, literary and historical subjects. This was not a universal public-school system: access, duration and curriculum varied, and the museum account does not justify assuming that all children, girls and boys, studied alike.

An authentic written sample appears on a copper coin minted in 1894: فيصل بن تركي بن سعيد امام مسقط وعمان. Arabic reads right to left. Editorial transliteration: Fayṣal bin Turkī bin Saʿīd, imām Masqaṭ wa-ʿUmān. Close translation: “Faisal bin Turki bin Said, Imam of Muscat and Oman.” It is the reverse legend of the Baisa al-Jalali, alongside English, not a sentence from everyday conversation. The title on a coin expresses rulership; it does not prove control of every place claimed.

Most healing happened long before a public biomedical system existed. A Ministry of Health-authored review documents oral plant knowledge passed by elders and healers, with remedies prepared as infusions, pastes, poultices or smoke; frankincense was among the plants used. Its evidence comes from later fieldwork, so it supports continuity of inherited practice rather than proving that every listed remedy had the same recipe in 1600. “Traditional” also does not automatically mean safe or clinically effective.

Nineteenth-century biomedicine arrived unevenly: visiting practitioners and court physicians came first, then a small British Agency hospital after 1861, the Arabian Mission from 1893 and a Muttrah clinic in 1904. Services clustered around Muscat and often favoured troops, foreigners or elites before missionary care widened access. Cholera struck in 1821, 1864 and 1899; plague was reported in Muttrah in 1899-1900. The medical history links epidemic risk to population movement, poor sanitation and unreliable clean water. Fort baths existed, but a flush-toilet fairy had not visited every home.

sections.title: Two excellent kid facts, and the atlas’s misleading finish line

items.text: The Sultanah was built in Bombay in 1833 and sailed from Zanzibar to New York with an Omani envoy and gifts in 1840. The crossing took 87 days; two years later the ship carried another mission to London. A museum reconstruction also shows a nineteenth-century fishing badan with planks stitched using coconut rope. Kid challenge: imagine trusting your lunch, letters and diplomatic presents to a wooden ship for almost three months, with zero airport snacks.

In 1913 supporters of an elected Ibadi imam under Salim bin Rashid al-Kharusi rose against the sultan. Interior centres including Nizwa, Izki and Awabi came under their control, while British Indian troops and ships backed the sultan’s coastal position. The archive calls the movement a “rebellion”; the card names the competing political claim instead of treating the imperial label as the only viewpoint. This conflict was active when the atlas polygon stops in 1914.

ending.text: The oman atlas record ends in 1914, but Oman did not. Fighting between the coastal sultanate and the interior imamate continued; the 1920 Treaty of As Sib left the sultan governing Muscat and coastal towns and the imam governing an autonomous interior. Later consolidation, oil-era conflict and the 1970 change from “Sultanate of Muscat and Oman” to “Sultanate of Oman” belong with the later muscat-and-oman and oman-1945 cards. The dataset has no Oman record for 1914-1938, so its blank is a coverage gap, not a vanished country or people.
